clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: The collection works systematically through all twenty-four major and minor keys, pairing a free piece with a strict contrapuntal one in each.

clues.label: Places the composer lived and worked
clues.text: Almost the whole of the composer's working life was spent within a small radius of towns in central Germany. He never travelled outside German-speaking lands.

clues.label: A biographical detail
clues.text: At the time of writing the composer was Kapellmeister to a young prince at a small court whose Reformed worship had no use for elaborate church music. He turned instead to instrumental and keyboard writing, much of it for teaching.

clues.label: An anecdote
clues.text: As a young man the composer walked several hundred kilometres to hear a celebrated organist play, then overstayed his approved leave by months and was reprimanded on his return.

clues.label: An anecdote
clues.text: The four letters of the composer's surname spell a melodic motif in German notation - B flat, A, C, B natural - which he wrote into the unfinished final fugue of his last work. He fathered twenty children across two marriages, and several sons became well-known composers in their own right.

explanation.summary: A Reformed princely court, a career confined to central Germany, and a systematic tour of all twenty-four keys: Johann Sebastian Bach at Köthen.

points.text: The systematic tour of all twenty-four keys, prelude paired with fugue, is the organising idea of Das wohltemperirte Clavier.
A career confined to central Germany, with no foreign travel, is unusual among major Baroque composers and characteristic of Bach.

The court is Köthen, where Bach served Prince Leopold from 1717 to 1723. The dated title page of Book I places it there in 1722 — a common trap, since the more famous Leipzig years began only the following year.
The long walk was to Lübeck, to hear Dieterich Buxtehude.
In German notation B natural is written H, so B flat–A–C–B natural spells BACH. He used the motif as a subject in Die Kunst der Fuge, left incomplete at his death.
